message:
FACTS:
Halvorsen needs a supplier for the injection-molded housing for its T-series thermostats. Sales forecasts 400,000 units for 2027. Over the last two years, actual volumes were 310,000 (against a forecast of 420,000) and 290,000 (against a forecast of 410,000). Supplier A (Ohio): $3.40 per unit, 0.4% defect rate, 3-week lead time, one-time tooling cost of $85,000. Supplier B (Vietnam): $2.55 per unit, plus about $0.38 per unit in freight and duty, 1.8% defect rate, 11-week lead time, one-time tooling cost of $40,000. A defective housing is usually found at final assembly. Rework, including scrapped parts and labor, costs about $14 per defective unit. Because of B's longer lead time, operations estimates Halvorsen would need to hold about 8 more weeks of safety stock. Inventory carrying cost is 20% a year. Halvorsen's largest customer, Brightline Homes, buys about 35% of T-series volume. Brightline's contract, renewed last spring, requires that products meet USMCA regional-content rules, which the plastic housing would not meet if made in Vietnam. The government is reviewing tariffs on this category of products from Vietnam and is expected to decide in February 2027. One option under consideration is an additional 25% tariff on the declared value of the part. Engineering plans a redesign of the T-series for mid-2028 that will need new tooling, so tooling bought now will be used for about 18 months. The CFO has asked for a 10% reduction in the cost of goods sold for the T-series. The Quality Manager opposes Supplier B. She points to two field-failure recalls in 2023 that came from a different offshore supplier and cost Halvorsen $410,000. Supplier B has offered to pay for one of Halvorsen's quality engineers to spend a month at its plant during the production ramp-up. Both suppliers can start production by March 2027. Neither will accept a contract shorter than 12 months.

KEY:
1. At the forecast 400k units, B is cheaper on unit price by about $188k a year ($3.40 vs $2.93 landed), but extra rework (1.8% vs 0.4% at $14, about $78k) and inventory carrying costs reduce the gap to roughly $75k a year, and if volume follows recent history (about 300k), the advantage shrinks further. GOOD HANDLING: Calculates total landed cost, not just unit price; questions the 400k forecast against actual volumes; and shows how sensitive the result is to volume.
2. 35% of volume (Brightline) cannot come from Vietnam under the USMCA content clause, so B can supply at most about 65% of volume, and using both suppliers means paying for tooling twice. GOOD HANDLING: Notices the constraint, adjusts the comparison (B for at most 65% of volume, or A for everything), and works out the dual-sourcing cost.
3. A possible 25% tariff (about $0.64 per unit on $2.55) would put B's landed cost around $3.57, above A's $3.40, and the decision is due in February, after tooling is ordered but before production starts. GOOD HANDLING: Treats the tariff as a major scenario that could reverse the choice, and proposes a way to manage it (e.g., delay commitment, contract terms that adjust for tariffs, or choose A).
4. Tooling is used for only about 18 months because of the 2028 redesign, so the $45k tooling difference matters more than usual, and the 10% COGS target may not be reachable through the housing alone. GOOD HANDLING: Spreads tooling cost over 18 months and tells the CFO how much of the 10% target this choice can realistically deliver.

DOCUMENT:
**MEMO**

**To:** Director of Procurement, Halvorsen Controls
**From:** Strategic Sourcing
**Date:** November 13, 2026
**Re:** Supplier recommendation for the T-series thermostat housing

**Recommendation**

Award the T-series housing to Supplier A (Ohio) on a 12-month contract starting March 2027, with an option to extend to the mid-2028 redesign. Do not split volume with Supplier B now. Instead, invite B to quote on the redesigned housing once the February tariff decision is known.

**Why B cannot be the sole supplier**

Brightline Homes buys about 35% of T-series volume. Its contract requires USMCA regional content, and a housing made in Vietnam fails that rule. Using B for everything would put that contract at risk. The real choice is between two options:

- A for all volume, or
- A for Brightline's units and B for the rest.

**All-in cost per unit**

| | Supplier A | Supplier B |
|---|---|---|
| Price | $3.40 | $2.55 |
| Freight and duty | n/a | $0.38 |
| Rework (defect rate × $14) | $0.06 | $0.25 |
| Carrying cost of 8 extra weeks of safety stock | n/a | $0.09 |
| Tooling spread over 18 months | $0.19 | $0.09 |
| **Total** | **$3.65** | **$3.36** |
| **Total with the proposed 25% tariff** | **$3.65** | **$4.00** |

I planned on 300,000 units a year rather than the 400,000 forecast. Actual volumes fell 26–29% short of forecast in each of the last two years.

**Split sourcing barely pays off**

B could supply at most 65% of volume, about 290,000 units over 18 months. Leaving tooling aside, B costs $0.18 less per unit than A, which saves about $54,000. B's $40,000 tooling cost brings the net saving down to roughly $14,000 over the life of the program. Even if the 400,000 forecast holds, the net saving is only about $32,000.

That small saving carries three risks.

- **Tariff.** A 25% tariff on B's $2.55 declared value adds $0.64 per unit. B would then cost about $0.45 more than A on every unit, or roughly $90,000 a year. We would have to sign B's 12-month minimum in December, before the February decision is known.
- **Quality.** B's defect rate is 4.5 times A's. My $14 rework figure assumes every defect is caught at final assembly. One defect reaching customers could erase the saving many times over. The 2023 recalls cost $410,000. They came from a different supplier, so they are not evidence against B, but they show what a field failure costs. B's offer to host one of our quality engineers would help during the ramp-up, not afterward.
- **Responsiveness.** With an 11-week lead time, we would be slow to adjust when volumes miss forecast, which has happened in each of the last two years. Running two suppliers would also mean two sets of tooling and more work to manage.

**The CFO's 10% target**

Choosing a housing supplier will not reach the 10% COGS reduction. Even sourcing everything from B, which we cannot do, would cut housing cost by only about 8%. The housing is one part of total T-series COGS. Better ways to pursue the target:

- Negotiate A's price using a realistic 300,000-unit commitment and a term that runs to the redesign.
- Ask A to lower or spread out its $85,000 tooling charge.
- Set a cost target for the 2028 redesign and open the new tooling to competitive bids, including B and Mexican molders.

**Next steps**

Request A's best-and-final offer at 300,000 units by December 5. Order tooling by mid-December.
